hints.junior: main.js jumped from 210 KB to 380 KB gzipped after a merge touching five files — 'look at the code' doesn't tell you which import cost 170 KB.
hints.mid: A single gzipped-size number is a symptom, not a diagnosis — it says the bundle grew, not which dependency grew it.
hints.staff: Same shape as a memory leak — an aggregate metric moved, and the fix means switching from 'what's the number' to 'what's inside it.'

hints.junior: Toggle to the treemap and click through the boxes — the biggest one is the culprit, before you even click it.
hints.mid: Box area is proportional to gzipped size, same convention real analyzers use — the oversized module is visually obvious.
hints.staff: Real analyzers show the resolved path on hover — useful for spotting the same package bundled twice at two different versions.

hints.junior: A treemap draws every module as a box sized by bytes — a tiny helper is a tiny box, a fully-imported library is a big one.
hints.mid: Compare before/after treemaps and look for the box that appeared or grew — usually a dependency imported more broadly than intended.
hints.staff: Toggle stat/parsed/gzip size modes — a module can look huge in source but compress away, or the reverse; which mode matters depends what you're optimizing for.

hints.junior: Reading a treemap by hand finds one culprit — once you know the pattern, write a rule that catches it automatically next time.
hints.mid: A per-PR size budget in CI catches the regression, but only a treemap tells you which import to fix — a budget failure alone hands the investigation back to you.
hints.staff: Watch for the same module twice at different sizes — that's usually a duplicated transitive dependency; deduplicating it often recovers more size than any single import fix.

sections.junior: Hey! Today's case is about a bundle that grew by 170 kilobytes after a merge, and nobody could tell from the code which import caused it.
The fix is a bundle analyzer treemap: every module gets drawn as a box sized by how many bytes it actually takes up, so the oversized one is just visually obvious.
Toggle between a raw size number and the treemap, then click through the boxes to find which one is actually huge.
A total size number can't tell you what's inside it. Open the treemap, look for the biggest box, and click it before you guess.
